energy-density-scalar-field.title: Energy density for scalar field
energy-density-scalar-field.conceptual_definition: The formula describes the energy density of a scalar field, which is a fundamental concept in quantum field theory and cosmology. It quantifies the amount of energy stored per unit volume within a region of spacetime occupied by a scalar field. This energy density comprises two components: the kinetic energy density arising from the field's motion and the potential energy density associated with the field's configuration.
energy-density-scalar-field.intuitive_summary: The total energy stored per unit volume in a scalar field is the sum of its kinetic energy (how fast it's changing) and its potential energy (its inherent stored energy).
energy-density-scalar-field.interpretation: The equation $ho = 0$.5̇ͅ^2 + V describes the energy density, ho, of a scalar field. The first term, $0.5̇ͅ^2$, represents the kinetic energy density. Here, ̇ͅ represents the time derivative of the scalar field, ̇ͅ = ∂̇ͅ/∂t, which quantifies how rapidly the field is changing with respect to time. Squaring this rate and multiplying by 0.5 gives the kinetic energy density. The units for this term would be Joules per cubic meter ($J/m^3$). The second term, V, represents the potential energy density of the scalar field. This term depends on the value of the scalar field itself, often expressed as V(̇ͅ), and describes the 'potential well' in which the field resides. Its units are also Joules per cubic meter ($J/m^3$). The total energy density ho is the sum of these two contributions, indicating that energy can be stored in both the motion and the configuration of the scalar field.
energy-density-scalar-field.symmetry_origin: This formula arises from the Lagrangian density for a scalar field. The Lagrangian density, $\mathcal{L}$, for a free scalar field is typically given by $\mathcal{L} = 0.5\partial_{\mu}\phi\partial^{\mu}\phi - V(\phi)$, where $\phi$ is the scalar field, $V(\phi)$ is the potential energy density, and $\partial_{\mu}$ denotes the four-gradient. The energy density can be derived from the stress-energy tensor, $T_{\mu\nu}$, which is obtained by varying the action with respect to the metric. Specifically, the time-time component of the stress-energy tensor, $T_{00}$, corresponds to the energy density. For a scalar field, $T_{00} = 0.5\dot{\phi}^2 + V(\phi)$, where $\dot{\phi} = \partial_t\phi$ is the time derivative.
energy-density-scalar-field.limits_and_boundary: When the scalar field is static (i.e., $\dot{\phi} = 0$), the energy density is solely determined by the potential energy density, $\$rho = V$. In this limit, the energy density represents the 'vacuum energy' if the potential is at its minimum. Conversely, if the potential energy density is constant or negligible ($V \approx 0$) and the field is oscillating rapidly, the energy density is dominated by the kinetic term, $\rho \approx 0.5\dot{\phi}^2$. As the scalar field value or its time derivative approaches infinity, the energy density can become arbitrarily large, indicating a highly energetic state.

\\rho.name: Energy Density
\\rho.description: The amount of energy stored per unit volume in the scalar field.

\\dot{\\phi}.name: Time derivative of the scalar field
\\dot{\\phi}.description: The rate of change of the scalar field \(\phi\) with respect to time. This term represents the velocity of the field's configuration.

V.name: Potential Energy Density
V.description: The potential energy stored per unit volume in the scalar field, dependent on the field's value. It describes the intrinsic energy of the field's configuration.

torque-component.title: Component of torque
torque-component.conceptual_definition: The formula describes the component of the torque vector \b{T} in a specific direction, often represented by the indices \b{i} and \b{j}, which correspond to Cartesian coordinate axes. It quantifies the tendency of a force \b{F} to cause rotation around a point or axis, based on the position vector \b{r} from the pivot point to the point where the force is applied. Specifically, it calculates the antisymmetric part of the dyadic product of the position and force vectors.
torque-component.intuitive_summary: This formula calculates the rotational effect of a force component perpendicular to the lever arm, revealing the directional aspect of torque.
torque-component.interpretation: The formula for the component of torque, \b{T_{ij}} = r_i $F_j - r_j$ F_i, represents the contribution to the torque along a specific axis or plane defined by the indices \b{i} and \b{j}. Here, \b{r_i} and \b{r_j} are the components of the position vector \b{r} (e.g., in meters, m) from the pivot point to the point of force application, along the \b{i}-th and \b{j}-th Cartesian axes, respectively. Similarly, \b{F_j} and \b{F_i} are the components of the force vector \b{F} (e.g., in Newtons, N) acting at that point, along the \b{j}-th and \b{i}-th axes. The term \b{r_i F_j} represents the torque component generated by the \b{j}-th component of force acting at a position characterized by the \b{i}-th component of the position vector, and \b{r_j F_i} represents the corresponding component from the swapped indices. The difference between these two terms captures the net rotational effect in the plane defined by the \b{i} and \b{j} directions, effectively yielding the magnitude of the torque component perpendicular to both \b{r} and \b{F} when considering the cross product formulation. This expression specifically isolates the antisymmetric part of the tensor formed by the position and force vectors.
torque-component.symmetry_origin: This formula arises from the definition of torque as the cross product of the position vector and the force vector, \b{\gamma T} = \b{r} × \b{F}. When expressed in terms of Cartesian components, the \b{ij}-th component of the torque tensor is given by \b{T_{ij}} = ̀_{ijk} r_k F_l ̀_{klm} where ̀ is the Levi-Civita symbol. Alternatively, and more directly related to the given formula, \b{T_{ij}} can be viewed as the component of the torque vector in the direction perpendicular to the \b{i} and \b{j} axes, which results from the antisymmetric nature of the cross product. This formulation emphasizes the antisymmetric property of the stress tensor or the resulting torque tensor, which is crucial in mechanics and electromagnetism. It is also related to the conservation of angular momentum, where a net torque results in a change in angular momentum.
torque-component.limits_and_boundary: If the position vector \b{r} is zero (i.e., \b{r_i} = \b{r_j} = 0), the torque component \b{T_{ij}} will be zero, as no force can induce rotation if it is applied at the pivot point. If the force \b{F} is zero (i.e., \b{F_i} = \b{F_j} = 0), the torque component \b{T_{ij}} will also be zero, as no torque is generated without a force. If the force is parallel to the position vector (i.e., \b{r_i F_j} = \b{r_j F_i}), the torque component \b{T_{ij}} will be zero, indicating that a force applied radially does not cause rotation. As the position vector or force components tend towards infinity, the torque component can also tend towards infinity, provided the components are not in a canceling relationship.

eikonal-equation.title: Eikonal Equation
eikonal-equation.conceptual_definition:
The Eikonal equation, in its relativistic form presented as \(\eta^{\mu
u} \partial_\mu S \partial_
u $S = -m^2$ c^2\), describes the short-wavelength limit of wave propagation in a medium or spacetime. It relates the gradient of the eikonal function, \(S\), to the local properties of the medium, represented by the metric tensor \(\eta^{\mu
u}\), and the intrinsic properties of the wave, characterized by its mass \(m\). In essence, it governs how wave fronts propagate, determining the direction and speed of phase velocity, and can be seen as a relativistic generalization of Fermat's principle of least time for wave optics.
eikonal-equation.intuitive_summary: This equation dictates how wave fronts move by relating the wave's phase gradient to its intrinsic properties and the structure of spacetime.
eikonal-equation.interpretation:
The equation \(\eta^{\mu
u} \partial_\mu S \partial_
u $S = -m^2$ c^2\) is a fundamental equation in relativistic wave physics, particularly in the context of geometrical optics and the WKB approximation. The term \(S\) is the eikonal, a scalar function whose gradient represents the phase of the wave. Specifically, \(\partial_\mu S\) is the four-gradient of the eikonal, which is related to the wave's four-wavevector \($k_\mu = \partial_\mu$ S\). The tensor \(\eta^{\mu
u}\) is the Minkowski metric tensor in flat spacetime, with signature \((+,-,-,-)\) or \((- ,+,+,+)\). The expression \(\eta^{\mu
u} \partial_\mu S \partial_
u S\) is the invariant magnitude squared of the four-wavevector, often written as \(k^\mu k_\mu\). This term is related to the dispersion relation of the wave. For massive particles, \(m\) is the rest mass of the particle (in SI units: kg), and \(c\) is the speed of light in vacuum (in SI units: m/s). The term \(-m^2 c^2\) represents the mass-shell condition for relativistic particles, where \(E^2 - (pc)^2 = (mc^2)^2\) is reformulated in terms of the four-momentum \($p_\mu = \hbark_\mu = \hbar$ \partial_\mu S\) as \(p^\mu p_\mu = (mc)^2\), and after absorbing \(\hbar\) into \(S\) (effectively setting \(\$hbar=1\$) in natural units or being careful with units), this becomes the structure seen. The equation thus connects the geometry of wave propagation (via \(\partial_\mu S\) and \(\eta^{\mu
u}\)) to the intrinsic physical properties of the wave (via \(m\) and \(c\)).
eikonal-equation.symmetry_origin: This equation arises from the short-wavelength limit of relativistic wave equations, such as the Klein-Gordon equation for massive scalar fields. By applying the WKB (Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin) approximation, which assumes that the wave function varies rapidly in space and time, one can derive this eikonal equation. It represents a conservation law related to the phase of the wave, and its form is dictated by Lorentz invariance, reflecting the requirement that the equation should be the same for all inertial observers.
eikonal-equation.limits_and_boundary: In the limit of zero mass \(m \to 0\), the equation simplifies to \(\eta^{\mu\nu} \partial_\mu S \partial_\nu $S = 0\$). This is the eikonal equation for massless waves, such as photons. In this case, the wave propagates along null geodesics, meaning the four-wavevector is always light-like. As the wavelength becomes infinitely long (low frequency and small wavevector), the eikonal approximation breaks down, and the full wave equation must be considered.

\\(\\eta^{\\mu\\nu}\\).name: Minkowski Metric Tensor
\\(\\eta^{\\mu\\nu}\\).description: The Minkowski metric tensor describes the geometry of flat spacetime in special relativity. It is a symmetric tensor used to raise and lower spacetime indices and define the invariant interval between two spacetime points. Its components depend on the chosen coordinate system but its form ensures Lorentz invariance. For instance, in Cartesian coordinates with signature (+,-,-,-), \(\eta^{\mu\nu} = \text{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1)\).

\\(S\\).name: Eikonal
\\(S\\).description: The eikonal is a scalar function that describes the phase of a wave. The gradient \(\partial_\mu S\) represents the four-wavevector of the wave, which is related to its momentum and energy. In optics, \(S\) is analogous to the phase of light, and its level surfaces are the wave fronts.

\\(\\partial_\\mu\\).name: Spacetime Gradient Operator
\\(\\partial_\\mu\\).description: This is the covariant derivative operator with respect to spacetime coordinates. \(\partial_\mu = (\frac{1}{c}\frac{\partial}{\partial t}, \frac{\partial}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial}{\partial z})\) in a flat spacetime with specific signature conventions. It acts on scalar fields to produce four-vectors.

\\(m\\).name: Rest Mass
\\(m\\).description: The rest mass of the particle or wave, representing its intrinsic inertial mass when it is at rest in its own reference frame. It is a fundamental property of the entity described by the wave.

\\(c\\).name: Speed of Light in Vacuum
\\(c\\).description: The speed of light in vacuum, a fundamental physical constant that represents the maximum speed at which all energy, matter, and information in the universe can travel. Its value is approximately \(299,792,458\) meters per second.

conservation-of-stress-energy-tensor.title: Conservation of Stress-Energy Tensor
conservation-of-stress-energy-tensor.conceptual_definition: The Conservation of the Stress-Energy Tensor, represented by the equation ∂^a T_{ab} = 0, is a fundamental principle in physics, particularly in general relativity and classical field theories. It states that the total stress-energy within any closed system remains constant, meaning that stress-energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed. This tensor equation encapsulates the conservation of energy, momentum, and stress in a relativistic and covariant manner. It is the relativistic generalization of the conservation of energy and momentum laws found in Newtonian physics.
conservation-of-stress-energy-tensor.intuitive_summary: The divergence of the stress-energy tensor is zero, signifying the local conservation of energy and momentum.
conservation-of-stress-energy-tensor.interpretation: The equation ∂^a T_{ab} = 0 describes the local conservation of stress-energy. The term ∂^a, representing the four-divergence, acts on the stress-energy tensor, denoted by $T_{ab}$. The stress-energy tensor is a rank-2 tensor that encapsulates the density and flux of energy and momentum in spacetime. Specifically, $T_{00}$ represents the energy density (in $J/m^3$), $T_{0i}$ represents the momentum density in the i-th direction (in kg/(m^2s)), $T_{i0}$ represents the energy flux in the i-th direction (in J/(m^2s)), and $T_{ij}$ represents the momentum flux in the j-th direction across a surface normal to the i-th direction, which also includes pressure and shear stress (in kg/(ms^2)). The condition ∂^a T_{ab} = 0 implies that for any infinitesimal volume element in spacetime, the rate of change of stress-energy within that volume is precisely balanced by the net flux of stress-energy into or out of that volume. This means that energy and momentum are locally conserved: they are not spontaneously created or destroyed, but rather transported through spacetime.
conservation-of-stress-energy-tensor.symmetry_origin: This conservation law arises from the fact that the laws of physics are generally covariant, meaning they do not depend on the choice of spacetime coordinates. Specifically, in the context of general relativity, the vanishing of the divergence of the stress-energy tensor is a consequence of the symmetries of spacetime, particularly the invariance under coordinate transformations (diffeomorphisms). The Einstein field equations, $G_{ab} = \frac{8\gamma ̇}{c^4} T_{ab}$, relate the curvature of spacetime (represented by the Einstein tensor $G_{ab}$) to the distribution of stress-energy. The Bianchi identities for the Einstein tensor, ∂^a G_{ab} = 0, combined with the field equations, directly imply the conservation of stress-energy ∂^a T_{ab} = 0.
conservation-of-stress-energy-tensor.limits_and_boundary: In the limit of empty spacetime where there is no matter or energy (i.e., $T_{ab} = 0$), the equation trivially holds true. In a flat spacetime (Minkowski spacetime) with no gravitational sources, the stress-energy tensor conservation reduces to the familiar conservation of energy and momentum for ordinary fields and particles. As spacetime curvature becomes significant, the interpretation of energy and momentum conservation becomes more complex due to the pseudo-tensor nature of gravitational energy-momentum, but the local conservation law ∂^a T_{ab} = 0 remains a fundamental principle for the stress-energy of matter and non-gravitational fields.

∂^a.name: Four-divergence Operator
∂^a.description: The four-divergence operator in spacetime. In Cartesian coordinates, it is defined as ∂^a = (∂/∂t, ∇), where ∂/∂t is the time derivative and ∇ is the gradient operator in spatial dimensions. It represents the rate of change of a quantity over spacetime. Its units are inverse length (1/m) because it operates on quantities with dimensions of length (like position or time in relativistic units).

T_{ab}.name: Stress-Energy Tensor
T_{ab}.description: The stress-energy tensor is a symmetric rank-2 tensor that describes the density, flux, and pressure of energy and momentum in spacetime. The index 'a' runs from 0 to 3, representing time and spatial dimensions, and similarly for index 'b'. The units are typically Joules per cubic meter (J/m^3) when considering energy density, but other components have units related to momentum density (kg/(m^2s)) and stress (kg/(ms^2)).

0.name: Zero
0.description: Represents the zero value, indicating that the four-divergence of the stress-energy tensor is identically zero, signifying conservation.
